title: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: A Report of a Rare X-Linked Disorder.

reviewer.method: Read entire structured text and fresh six-page PDF layout extraction, including endmatter and twelve references. Inspected both figure panels and all rows/reference ranges of Tables 1–2 as pixels. Individually compared the sole packet, its allele and all twelve phenotype assertions.

audit.exposure_note: Parent previously saw compact-cohort aggregate results; no WAS per-case rank consulted for this review. Post-inference and not blinded.

genotype.statement: Source reports c.756G>A/p.Trp252Ter in exon 8 by whole-exome sequencing, matching packet coding/protein change. Male X-linked context is compatible with hemizygosity.

segregation.statement: The source reports no similar family complaints but does not report parental molecular testing or maternal carrier status.

phase.statement: One X-linked allele is reported in a male; no two-allele trans/cis question arises from this packet.

causal_confidence.statement: The discussion explicitly calls c.756G>A/p.Trp252Ter likely pathogenic, whereas the packet records PATHOGENIC. The source authors diagnose WAS from WES and the clinical findings, but the packet overstates their reported classification.

evidence.locator: Case presentation, PDF pages 1–4; Discussion, page 5

limitations: This is a source-classification discrepancy, not a new ACMG assessment or evidence that WAS is the wrong diagnosis.
No segregational or patient-specific WASP functional assay is supplied. Reference 9 is a general OMIM database publication, not an allele-specific experiment.

phenotype_completeness.statement: All twelve features reviewed. Most describe explicit observations; iron deficiency, overall marrow hypercellularity, persistent-fever coding and myelodysplasia require qualifications because the source describes suggestive findings or limited duration.

limitations: Terminology is the source authors’ description; no independent clinical examination.
Full reading is not laboratory replication or independent clinical truth. This audit is post-inference with prior aggregate-result exposure.

Source says lymphocyte subset analysis was normal, yet Table 2 gives CD3 1815 below its lower limit 1900, CD3 percentage 37 below 49, CD8 245 below 500, CD19 percentage 13.20 below 14 and lymphocyte percentage 39.60 below 41. These internal discrepancies are retained, not silently resolved.
The authors’ growth-percentile assertion was read but not independently recomputed from growth-reference charts.
Negative unspecified molecular testing does not rule out every marrow disorder. The morphology was viewed, but no independent pathology diagnosis is claimed.
No supplementary files are listed; absence of raw exome, segregation and protein-function data remains a scientific limitation even though all published components were read.
